children: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday blamed Friday's air-travel outage that caused havoc at airports nationwide on work being done to replace copper wires with fiber ones at a single remote facility.
He pointed the finger at the work of contractor L3Harris, which either installed a faulty router or was "not doing great work for us," Duffy told reporters on Saturday.
"So what we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence," Duffy said. "Frankly, we're going to hold people accountable."

L3Harris, which has worked with the Federal Aviation Administration for decades, said that it is supporting the FAA's investigation. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," it said.

The disruptions Friday, after authorities halted air traffic for more than four hours, left planes and crew members out of place for their next flights, and undoing the chaos caused by the ground stop is expected to take days.
"Operations are slowly returning to normal this morning," Duffy posted to social media. "Planes are pushing back, taxiing, and taking off, and it is safe to fly."

Nationwide ground stops like the one on Friday are an extraordinary measure. The last one happened in 2023, when an outage of another system led the FAA to halt all departures across the country. Before that, the last ground stop was issued in 2001 in response to the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.

More than 6,000 flights were canceled on Saturday, and as of Saturday evening, airlines had already scrapped 530 U.S. flights on Sunday. On Friday after the ground stop, about 9,000 commercial flights were canceled, as well as about 3,000 private jet flights. Saturday's slate of college football games was scrambled by the chaos as teams were planning to travel late Friday.

At New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport on Saturday, flights were canceled minutes before boarding was supposed to start, with announcers citing staffing issues. Airlines, including United, Delta and American, said they would waive ticket-change fees and were scrambling to get pilots and flight attendants in position to operate flights. Airports encouraged people to check their flight status to avoid long wait times.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said there was no evidence that the disruption was caused by AI-related issues or "anything nefarious." He said after observing instability in the system, authorities ordered the ground stop "out of an abundance of caution." Airline schedules should be back to normal Sunday night, he said.
"I do think the worst is behind us, but we still do have a significant amount of recovery work to do," Bedford said.

The work L3Harris was doing Friday was "routine maintenance" at an undisclosed "remote location" that shouldn't have caused major disruptions, Duffy said. But after the router was changed, it flooded other routers in the air-traffic control system with 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, he said, causing issues with airplane communications and radar feeds.
"When we see that," Duffy said, "we shut down the airspace, and we do it safely."
Duffy pleaded with Congress to approve funding to upgrade the country's air-traffic system, an overhaul he said would cost $50 billion. Without it, he said outages could happen again.
"If we don't make these upgrades, we have a less safe system," Duffy said Saturday. "We can't continue on technology of the '80s."
